report:
## Your sister is right — the evidence strongly supports "yes"

**The core evidence:** The pivotal FREEDOM trial (Cummings et al., *NEJM* 2009), a large, international, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of over 7,800 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, found that denosumab given every 6 months for 36 months reduced the risk of new vertebral fractures by **68%**, along with reductions in hip fractures (~40%) and nonvertebral fractures (~20%) compared with placebo (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa0809493). This is a high-quality, well-powered RCT — the gold standard of evidence — and it's the trial that led to FDA approval of Prolia.

**Long-term data confirm durability:** The FREEDOM Extension study followed patients for up to 10 years and found that continuous denosumab treatment sustained low vertebral fracture rates and produced progressive gains in bone mineral density, with continuing reductions in nonvertebral fracture risk (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8799550/). Fracture incidence remained low year after year rather than rebounding.

**Independent, non-manufacturer sources agree:** A summary from the American Academy of Family Physicians states plainly that "denosumab appears to be effective in reducing the risk of vertebral and nonvertebral fractures in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis," without increasing risks of cancer or death (https://www.aafp.org/afp/2019/0501/od1). TheNNT.com, an independent evidence-review site skeptical of over-stated drug claims, reaches the same conclusion after evaluating the trial data.

**One important caveat:** Evidence also shows that *stopping* denosumab abruptly can lead to a rebound loss of bone density and, in some cases, multiple vertebral fractures shortly after discontinuation — so ongoing/continuous use or careful transition to another therapy matters.

**Bottom line:** Yes — high-quality randomized trial evidence, confirmed by long-term follow-up and independent reviewers, supports that denosumab (Prolia) meaningfully reduces vertebral (and other) fracture risk in osteoporosis, provided treatment continuity is maintained.
